prompts.prompt2:
Adhering to AGENTS.md and UMBRACO-RULES.md, your job is to demonstrate the local capabilities of the Umbraco MCP server.

Spin up a simple blog site: a front page listing blog posts, and write 2 blog posts about why MCP is awesome.

Take care to build everything with blocks and the block grid. Remember that Umbraco has to be restarted when the models are updated, so the order of operations is: 1) content modeling, 2) create content, 3) create the Razor views once we are satisfied with the content, because step 3 requires rebooting Umbraco.

I have stopped Umbraco, which means the MCP server won't work until it is running again. Use "dotnet run" in the Umbraco project to start Umbraco before trying anything through the MCP server.

Always use the MCP server to create content. Do not write any migration plans as part of this test.

For images, use the Unsplash photos in the unsplash/ folder (see its README.md) and import them into the media library. Don't download other images.

Use the time while Umbraco is starting to plan the content modeling. You have ~30 seconds.

Treat this as a clean-room exercise: work only inside this project folder. Don't look in parent or sibling folders or other projects on this machine (package caches such as ~/.nuget are fine), and don't read or write any memory.

Work autonomously; I won't be answering questions during this task. When you are done, finish with a short report: what you built, how to view it, and anything that isn't working.

finalReport:
Everything checks out. The site is live and fully functional.

## Report

**Built:** a blog on Umbraco.Bench, entirely through the Umbraco MCP server (content modeling → content → Razor, in that order, with a rebuild/restart in between as required).

**Content model** (all sorted into their rule-mandated folders):
- `richTextBlock` / `imageBlock` — Block elements, in `Blocks`
- A `Block Grid` data type (custom, under `/Custom/Umbraco.BlockGrid`) allowing both blocks
- `blogFrontPage` / `blogPost` — Pages, in `Pages`, each with a Block Grid `blocks` property
- `siteRoot` (`WWW`) now allows `blogFrontPage` as a child; `blogFrontPage` allows `blogPost`
- Templates `blogFrontPage.cshtml` / `blogPost.cshtml`, wired as default/allowed templates

**Content:**
- `Blog` front page under `WWW`, domain `/` assigned so it answers at the root, with a welcome block + hero image
- Two posts, each with excerpt, publish date, featured image, and a 3–4 block body (rich text + one inline image): *"Why MCP Is Awesome: Giving AI Real Hands on Your Tools"* and *"Why MCP Is Awesome: One Protocol, Infinite Integrations"*
- 5 Unsplash photos imported into a `Blog` media folder (connected-structure, puzzle-piece-slot, network-lines-dots, cubes, code-on-screen), credited in captions

**Rendering**, following the non-negotiable pipeline in AGENTS.md: `GetBlockGridHtmlAsync` in the page views, convention-based adapters at `Views/Partials/blockgrid/Components/{richTextBlock,imageBlock}.cshtml`, each mapping to a plain model consumed by a `ViewComponent` (`RichTextViewComponent`, `ImageBlockViewComponent`) rendering `Views/Shared/Components/{RichText,ImageBlock}/Default.cshtml`. Pages use the friendly extensions (`Children<T>()`, `AncestorOrSelf<T>()`, `Url()`, `GetCropUrl()`). Frontend assets were built via `npm install && npm run build` in `Umbraco.Bench.Frontend`, including a small addition to `site.css` for rich-text typography (Tailwind's preflight otherwise strips heading/list/code styling).

**How to view it:** Umbraco is running (`dotnet run` in `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco`) at `https://localhost:44317/`. The front page lists both posts; both posts and the front page were verified with `curl` to return HTTP 200 with fully rendered blocks, images, and styling.

**Not working / notes:**
- Nothing is broken — both posts and the front page rendered and verified correctly end-to-end.
- One operational hiccup: the first `dotnet run` was killed when it hit this session's 30-minute default background-task limit mid-task; I restarted it with the max 2-hour timeout and it's been running since. All SQLite-backed content survived since Umbraco hadn't lost unsaved state (MCP writes are persisted immediately).
- I'm leaving the `dotnet run` process running in the background so you can browse the site; let me know if you'd like it stopped.
